name: Hydrogen peroxide ingestion

card.summary: Drinking diluted food-grade hydrogen peroxide, promoted in fringe wellness circles as a way to oxygenate the body and cleanse it, with skin and general appearance among the claimed benefits.
card.note: Poison-center and case literature documents gas embolism, gastrointestinal injury and neurological harm from ingestion, especially of concentrated solutions.

quick.overview:
Hydrogen peroxide ingestion is the practice of drinking diluted hydrogen peroxide, usually sold as a food-grade solution, on the theory that it releases oxygen in the body and supports health, which proponents link to clearer skin and better energy and general appearance.

It belongs to the broader tradition of oxygen and bio-oxidative therapies. Medical literature on oral hydrogen peroxide consists mostly of poisoning case reports and poison-center series rather than trials of benefit.
quick.how: Proponents describe diluting the solution in water and drinking small amounts; the same circles also discuss peroxide baths and intravenous forms. This wiki gives no preparation or amounts. Household 3 percent peroxide and stronger solutions sold as food grade differ greatly in strength.
quick.risks: Case reports describe oxygen gas bubbles entering the portal vein and bloodstream, stomach and oesophageal injury, seizures, strokes and death after ingestion, most severely with concentrated 35 percent solutions. Hyperbaric oxygen has been used to treat gas embolism. Poison control services and emergency physicians treat ingestion as a poisoning risk.

lead: Hydrogen peroxide ingestion refers to drinking diluted hydrogen peroxide, commonly sold as a food-grade product, as a wellness practice. Proponents of oxygen or bio-oxidative therapy argue that peroxide releases oxygen in the body and supports tissue health, and they sometimes connect it with skin clarity, energy and a healthier look.[1][2][3]

The idea has circulated for decades in alternative-health communities; fitness forums in the mid-2000s discussed peroxide baths and intravenous bio-oxidative therapy among athletes, citing figures from strength-coaching sites.[4][5]

Medical literature on swallowing peroxide is dominated by toxicology: poison-centre case series and individual reports describe gas embolism, gastrointestinal injury and neurological damage, particularly with concentrated solutions.[6][7][8][9] A 2009 oncology review covers oxygen therapies as a group.[10]

chain: Believers say it releases oxygen into tissues
Proponents expect better skin, energy and overall look
angle.text: Practitioners claim oxygenation of the body improves vitality and skin appearance. The effect on looks is claimed rather than documented, while harms from ingestion are well described.

infobox: Oral intake of diluted food-grade solution
FDA classifies it as generally recognised as safe as an antimicrobial agent, not as an oral remedy[11]

paras: Hydrogen peroxide is a common disinfectant and bleach that decomposes into water and oxygen. Wikipedia notes consumer solutions are typically 3 to 6 percent, while concentrations above about 40 percent are treated as hazardous.[11] Oral peroxide practice uses diluted food-grade solutions of higher strength than household bottles, which is why poison-centre series focus on 35 percent ingestions.[6]
Believers describe it under the heading of bio-oxidative medicine, the addition of oxygen to tissues.[5]

A 2005 T Nation thread asks about bio-oxidative therapy, including intravenous H2O2 and warm baths with peroxide, and a related thread quotes a strength coach on the theory that peroxide adds oxygen to the tissues.[4][5] Proponents argue small amounts are harmless; posts in that thread describe the amounts as modest.[5]
Physicians report that purported benefits being sought are tied to increased oxygen delivered to the bloodstream.[8]

No clinical trials of ingested hydrogen peroxide for appearance or health benefit are cited here. The human literature is toxicology. A poison-centre series of 11 portal venous gas embolism cases, mostly accidental 35 percent ingestions, reported resolution with hyperbaric oxygen in most patients.[6] Case reports describe near-fatal ingestion with seizure and respiratory arrest,[12] upper gastrointestinal injury after ingestion for health purposes,[8] extensive portal venous gas,[9] and blindness from embolic strokes that improved with hyperbaric oxygen.[7] A separate oncology review describes oxygen therapies generally.[10]

The 2010 poison-centre review states that concentrated peroxide ingestion has been associated with venous and arterial gas embolism, haemorrhagic gastritis, bleeding, shock and death, and that low concentrations are generally considered benign.[6] A 2017 case report says intentional high-concentration ingestion for health reasons has gained popularity in some patient groups.[8] Wikipedia lists hazard labelling for concentrated peroxide including severe burns and harm if swallowed.[11]

timeline.event: Louis Jacques Thenard prepares hydrogen peroxide.[11]
Annals of Emergency Medicine reports a near-fatal ingestion of 35 percent peroxide.[12]
Poison-centre series on portal venous gas embolism after peroxide ingestion.[6]
Case report of blindness after peroxide ingestion with recovery after hyperbaric oxygen.[7]

lore.intro: Peroxide appears in older fitness-forum threads as part of bio-oxidative or oxygen therapy discussions.[4][5]

claims.claim: Peroxide adds oxygen to tissues and aids recovery or vitality
claims.believers: Posts cite a strength coach describing bio-oxidative medicine as adding oxygen directly to tissues.[5]
claims.experts: Emergency-medicine reports document oxygen gas embolism rather than benefit after ingestion.[6][8]

claims.claim: Baths and dilute use are safe
claims.believers: Forum posters say the amounts used are small and unlikely to hurt.[5]
claims.experts: Reviews note low concentrations are generally benign while concentrated ones have caused severe toxicity.[6]
